source_refs.note: Topic 23.1.1 (PDF 102-103); Figure 23.1 is redrawn. The book's 'preparation of ethanol' and 'Methanol, HCHO' are read as ethanal and methanal, and formalin's 'fishy' smell is given as sharp; see the coverage register.

blocks.text: Aldehydes are made by oxidising primary alcohols with acidified K2Cr2O7 or acidified KMnO4: CH3CH2OH + [O] -> CH3CHO + H2O (K2Cr2O7 + H2SO4(aq), heat).

To prepare ethanal, acidified K2Cr2O7 is added dropwise to warm ethanol, and the ethanal is distilled off as soon as it forms. This prevents its further oxidation to ethanoic acid. The temperature is kept above the boiling point of ethanal (acetaldehyde) but below that of ethanol, which boils at a higher temperature. Pure ethanal is obtained by redistillation.

blocks.alt: Apparatus: acidified K2Cr2O7 drips from a dropping funnel into warm ethanol in a flask standing in a warm water bath; a thermometer reads the vapour temperature; the vapour passes along a water-cooled condenser (water in at the bottom, out at the top) and ethanal collects in a test tube.
blocks.caption: Distilling off ethanal as it forms (original diagram after Figure 23.1).
blocks.long_description: Ethanal boils at a much lower temperature than ethanol, so with the water bath hotter than ethanal's boiling point but cooler than ethanol's, the ethanal escapes as vapour as soon as it forms and is condensed and collected before the dichromate can oxidise it further.

blocks.title: Methanal
blocks.text: Methanal, HCHO, is a gas at room temperature. It is often met as a 40% aqueous solution called formalin, which has a sharp, unpleasant smell and is used to preserve biological specimens. Other short-chain aldehydes and ketones are liquids.
